newsitem.title: SWAZILAND: Donors eye strike in usually stable Swaziland.
newsitem.headline: Donors eye strike in usually stable Swaziland.

text.p: Swaziland's image as a haven of peaceful stability is wavering as a national strike to force quicker political reform continued for a third day on Wednesday, closely watched by donors and investors, diplomats said.
An absolute monarchy with a population of some 900,000, Swaziland has historically been seen as a stable country ripe for foreign investment in a region beset by political turmoil.
But that is changing as neighbouring South Africa -- which absorbs over half of Swaziland's exports -- moves towards three years of democracy.
The head of the European Union's delegation in Swaziland, Gabriel Lee, said in an interview that donors and investors were watching developments in the kingdom very closely.
"If the situation deteriorates to a point where investment and economic support are not conducive to success, there will be a rethink by donors and investors," he said.
"This strike (if prolonged) will create a climate that will frighten away investors, who will go to other African countries where the climate is right," Lee added.

As Swaziland's largest aid donor, the EU is intending to spend around 250 million rand ($55.8 million) there over the next four years. About 70 percent of that is earmarked for agriculture and rural development.

The vital sugar and timber export industries have been hardest hit by the union-led strike to demand the repeal of a 1973 royal decree which banned political activity and vested state powers in the monarch.
Prompted by a violent strike in 1996, a review commission was set up by reigning King Mswati III to make recommendations on moves towards a constitutional democracy.

But the commission, criticised for being unrepresentative and for its slowness, is not due to put forward proposals until about two years' time. Despite this, one Western diplomat said it was probably the only workable way to bring about reform.
"It is perfectly clear that despite all criticism internally and externally, the king is taking Swaziland on a process of reform, and strikes to force the pace are largely irrelevant," he added.

But he suggested the labour unrest could be viewed bleakly by cautious investors, saying: "Foreign countries are watching with concern what is going on here, because it could come to affect foreign investment."
The EU's Lee said while there had been no major foreign investment in the kingdom since 1991, a number of smaller companies had invested and existing companies were ploughing back profits.
"It is a healthy sign to potential investors to see current investors putting their profits back into the country," he said.
